Rather than empirically re-testing Baron et al.'s eyewitness task-importance by task-difficulty interaction, the authors derive H2 from the general economic principle that piece-rate rewards for correct answers reduce conformity in the Asch line task, and never test or report an incentive-by-difficulty interaction in Section 4. The Discussion remark that an 8 percentage-point reduction in line-task errors 'sheds doubt on former results which predominately show the opposite effect, namely that incentives increase compliance [ 5 ,  6 ]' is a post-hoc literature contrast, not an empirical replication of Baron et al. decision.location: Section 2.1 Monetary incentives (line 99); see also Section 5 Conclusion and discussion (line 169)
decision.quote: Bhanot and Williamson [ 6 ] conducted online experiments (using Amazon Mechanical Turk) in which 391 participants answered 60 multiple-choice trivia-knowledge questions while the most popular answer was displayed at each question. Correct answers were incentivized randomly with $0, $1, $2 or $3 each in a within-subject design, i.e. randomized over trials, not over subjects. Bhanot and Williamson [ 6 ] found that monetary incentives increase the proportion of answers that align with the majority. Hence, the studies using incentives yield inconclusive and contradicting results: Particularly, Baron et al. [ 5 ] found both an accuracy-increasing and accuracy-decreasing effect of monetary incentives depending on task difficulty. Bhanot and Williamson [ 6 ] found an increased conformity rate, and Fujita and Mori [ 7 ] found that the conformity bias disappears in the individually incentivized condition. Overall, we follow the economic notion that monetary incentives matter and expect that rewards for nonconformity decrease group pressure (H 2 ).
decision.reason: Bhanot and Williamson (2020) [6] studied online Mechanical Turk herding on 60 multiple-choice trivia questions with trial-level within-subject monetary rewards. Franzen and Mader (2023) cite it as part of the conflicting prior literature motivating their between-subject piece-rate monetary incentive extension (H2) of Asch's face-to-face line-judgment paradigm (shipped row 6, Asch 1956). They do not empirically re-test Bhanot and Williamson's online trivia herding design or finding; mentioning [5, 6] in the Discussion as prior work showing opposite effects is a literature contrast rather than a replication test.

decision.quote: Fujita and Mori [ 7 ] analysed the effect of individual vs collective payoff in the Asch experiment. They found that the conformity effect disappears in the individually incentivized condition. However, also this study suffered from low sample sizes since there were only 10 subjects in the individualized minority incentive condition. Furthermore, Fujita and Mori [ 7 ] used the fMORI method and report that some subjects might have noticed the trick.
decision.reason: Fujita and Mori (2017) [7] is reviewed only in the Introduction and Section 2.1 as prior literature comparing individual versus collective payoffs in a confederate-free fMORI task to motivate the paper's monetary-incentive extension (H2) of Asch's confederate line-judgment task (shipped row 6, Asch 1956). The current study does not manipulate individual versus collective payoffs, does not use the fMORI paradigm, and never cites or compares results against Fujita and Mori (2017) in the Results or Discussion.

decision.location: Section 5. Conclusion and discussion (line 170); see also Sections 2.2-2.3 (lines 103, 108-112) and References (line 201)
decision.quote: Moreover, our study suggests that group pressure is not only influential in the simple line task but also when it comes to political opinions. We randomized the groups’ response to five different political statements and find an average conformity rate of 38%. Hence, these results suggest that the original finding of Asch can also be generalized to matters of opinion. This result is in line with former evidence by Crutchfield [ 8 ], and Mallinson and Hatemi [ 9 ]. However, both of these studies had only small sample sizes of 50 and 58 subjects respectively, which called for further replication studies. Finally, we measured the Big Five, intelligence, self-esteem and social approval. With the exception of openness, our study finds no support that these personality traits are statistically significantly related to the susceptibility of group pressure.
decision.reason: Addressing the prior objection and scope review: Crutchfield (1955) [8] is not merely generic background for an extension. Section 1 notes that replication of political-opinion conformity is needed, Section 2.2 details Crutchfield's specific experimental political-opinion conformity effects (36 and ~40 percentage-point increases under social pressure with n=50) to derive H3, Section 2.3 details Crutchfield's individual-difference correlates of conformity (intellectual competence, ego strength/self-esteem, need for social approval, and gender with N=50) to derive H4-H6, and Section 5 explicitly compares the current 38% political-opinion conformity result to Crutchfield [8] while stating that its small sample size (n=50) 'called for further replication studies.' The only shipped row (row 6: Asch 1956, 10.1037/h0093718) is Asch's perceptual line-judgment monograph, which is an entirely different work and author from Crutchfield (1955) in The American Psychologist (10: 191-198), and Target 7 (Mallinson & Hatemi 2018) is a separate 2018 political-discussion study.

Section 1 states that Mallinson and Hatemi [9] is the only other study investigating social conformity on political opinion formation and calls for 'further replications on the transferability from lines to a variety of political opinions', Section 2.2 reviews their specific experimental finding (38% vs. 8% opinion change on a political issue, n=58) to derive H3, Part 2 tests political-opinion conformity in N=202 subjects, and Section 5 directly compares the resulting 38% conformity rate with Mallinson and Hatemi [9] while stating that its small sample size (n=58) 'called for further replication studies.' decision.quote: Iscoe, Williams, and Harvey [ 10 ] exposed high school students (7 to 15 years) to group pressure in an acoustic task (counting metronome ticks), and approximated intelligence by subjects’ school records. They found no correlation of school records with conformity. Uchida et al. [ 31 ] studied 12 to 14 year-old high school students and assessed scholastic achievements by their school performance. They report that high achievers conformed less to the majority than low achievers. Hence, results of the effect of intelligence on conformity are inconclusive so far and the existing studies use indirect measures (school grades) but do not measure intelligence directly.
decision.reason: Iscoe, Williams, and Harvey (1964) [10] is cited only as background in the literature review to illustrate that prior studies of intelligence and conformity used indirect school-record proxies in children (in a metronome-counting task) with inconclusive results, motivating the authors' direct intelligence measure (Hagen Matrices Test) in their extension (H5) of the Asch experiment (shipped row 6, Asch 1956). The paper does not re-test Iscoe et al.'s child acoustic-task study and never mentions or compares against [10] in the Results or Discussion.
